title: Build the equipment: a furnace, an annealer and a glory hole
preface: Three pieces of studio equipment drawn up for a do-it-yourself build by someone who can weld and fabricate, with every part that goes into them. Options cover the electrical service (240 V single-phase, the two-hot-leg service most buildings have, or three-phase at 208 V or 240 V) and the fuel (natural gas or propane for the glory hole and for the gas furnace). The designs follow the shop this site documents (an electric furnace on silicon-carbide elements with an SCR, a gas glory hole on forced air, electric annealers on a ramp-soak controller) and the published do-it-yourself lineage of studio glass equipment. Quantities, sizes and prices are planning figures; every gas and high-current electrical connection is designed and inspected by licensed people to the code in force where you build.

phase.label: 240 V single-phase
phase.note: the ordinary two-hot-leg service (often called two-phase in a shop; it is one phase split in two); 208 V single-phase buildings follow the same parts with the 208 V arithmetic

phase.label: 208 V three-phase wye
phase.note: 120/208 V, four-wire; coils and element strings can use 120 V line-to-neutral or 208 V line-to-line

phase.label: 240 V three-phase delta
phase.note: three-wire delta, common in older industrial buildings; no neutral, so every load is line-to-line

fuel.label: natural gas
fuel.note: low-pressure service at 7 inches of water column at the appliance; a 2 psi service needs a pounds-to-inches regulator at each appliance

fuel.label: propane
fuel.note: 11 inches of water column at the appliance from a two-stage regulator at the tank; tank size is set by vaporization, not by volume

ng_pipe_cfh.note: Schedule 40 steel, natural gas 0.6 specific gravity, 0.5 inch water column drop, from the National Fuel Gas Code sizing table; verify against the edition in force

constants.propane_vaporization_note: A tank vaporizes propane only as fast as the air warms its wetted wall. As a planning rule (supplier charts govern): a 120 gal tank half full gives about 100,000 BTU/h at 20 F and 200,000 at 60 F; a 500 gal tank half full about 300,000 at 20 F and 600,000 at 60 F; a 1,000 gal tank roughly double. A gas furnace plus a glory hole in a cold climate is a 1,000 gal tank or a 500 gal tank with an electric vaporizer.

equipment.name: Furnace, 100 lb invested crucible
equipment.summary: A square, top-and-front-loading pot furnace: a 100 lb invested (fused-silica) crucible on a cast plinth inside a chamber 22 by 22 inches in plan and 30 inches tall, 2,800 F insulating firebrick hot face backed by fiber board and blanket, a cast refractory floor that can hold a lost pot, a 6 by 8 inch gathering port with a counterweighted cast door, and either four silicon-carbide elements through the side walls above the pot or a single forced-air burner firing tangentially at floor level with a damped flue in the lid. It melts and holds 100 lb of soda-lime at 2,100 to 2,150 F, fines at 2,300 F, and idles on about 6 to 8 kW or 70 to 100 thousand BTU/h when well built.

design.chamber: 22 x 22 in plan, 30 in tall; the crucible rim 18 in above the floor slab, the port sill 2 in above the rim, the elements 2 and 5 in above it; 3.5 in clearance pot to wall
design.walls: 2.5 in K-28 insulating firebrick (2,800 F) hot face, twelve courses, 2 in 2,300 F ceramic fiber board, 1 in 8 lb ceramic fiber blanket against the steel
design.floor: 3 in dense 3,000 F castable slab with a 1 in raised dam at the edges, over 2.5 in K-26 firebrick and 1 in fiber board; a 1 in drain notch at the front corner so a lost pot runs to a steel catch tray, not into the brick
design.plinth: cast 3,000 F dense castable disk, 15 in diameter, 4 in tall, with three 1 in setting feet so the pot sits level and air moves under the floor skin
design.roof: removable lid: 3 in cast 3,000 F castable slab in a 2 in angle pan, 2 in fiber board above it, lifting eyes; the gas option casts a 3 in flue with a sliding damper plate through it
design.port: 6 in wide x 8 in tall gathering port in the front wall, sill 2 in above the pot rim; a 3 in thick cast castable door block in a 1/4 in steel channel frame on a 1 in pivot pin, counterweighted to hang open or fall shut
design.shell: 2 x 2 x 3/16 in angle frame, 12 gauge skin, 1 in standoff air gap between skin and blanket at the sides for a cooler shell, legs 8 in, lifting eyes at the four top corners
design.outside: about 36 in wide, 36 in deep, 50 in tall to the lid top on 8 in legs, about 1,300 lb lined
design.electric: four silicon-carbide elements, 1 in diameter, 22 in hot zone, horizontal through the side walls 2 in above the pot rim (two per side), in two series pairs in parallel on single-phase or three series pairs in delta on three-phase, fed by a phase-angle SCR with a current limit, a safety contactor, a high-limit controller and a door interlock
design.gas: one forced-air burner of 120,000 to 200,000 BTU/h entering tangentially 3 in above the floor at the back corner, a cast burner block, a 3 in flue in the lid with a damper, a flame safeguard with a UV scanner, a pilot, and a gas train to the National Fuel Gas Code

build_notes: Weld the base rectangle and uprights square and flat; the brick lining does not forgive a racked box. Set the leveling feet before anything goes inside.

Lay 1 in blanket against the skin, then the 2 in board, then the brick, course by course with thin mortar joints and staggered bonds; cut the element sleeve holes (electric) or the burner block pocket (gas) as the courses reach them, not afterwards.

Cast the floor slab in place over the board and backup brick with its dam and drain notch, vibrating out the air; cast the plinth, the door block and the lid slab in forms the same day. Keep every casting damp under plastic for 24 hours.

Dry the castables on the furnace's own first fire: 50 F an hour to 250 F and hold 6 hours, 50 F an hour to 500 F and hold 6 hours, then 100 F an hour to 1,000 F, then to working temperature. Steam that cannot escape spalls the slab; patience is cheaper than castable.

Electric: set the elements in their sleeves with 1/2 in of free length outside each wall, straps on the cold ends, leads in the guards; check each string's cold resistance with a meter and record it on the inside of the enclosure door with the date.

Gas: fire the burner first outside the furnace into open air, set the orifice and air for a blue flame with a short yellow tip, then into the block; the damper is set so a match flame at the port leans gently out.

First pot: follow the crucible maker's pre-heat, usually 50 F an hour to 1,000 F and 100 F an hour above it, with the pot empty; charge in 10 to 15 lb lots at 2,100 F or above, never into a cold pot, and fine at 2,300 F for six to eight hours before the first working day.

equipment.name: Annealer, 30 x 24 x 24 in front loader
equipment.summary: A front-loading electric annealer with a 30 in wide, 24 in deep, 24 in tall chamber lined with 2.5 in insulating firebrick and 1 in fiber board, four coiled iron-chrome-aluminium elements in grooved brick on the side and back walls, a hinged brick door with a rope seal, a ramp-soak controller driving solid-state relays through a safety contactor with an independent high limit, and a door switch that cuts power. Rated 7.2 kW: it reaches 950 F in about an hour from cold with the shelf loaded and holds within 5 F. A 20 x 20 x 20 in version with the same parts at 4.8 kW is noted where the quantities differ.

build_notes: Build the box, then dry-fit the brick before mortar: a 30 in wall is 3.33 bricks, so plan the cuts to land at the back corners where the grooves do not run.
Cut the element grooves with a diamond or masonry blade on a track; round every corner with a rasp so the coil lies without kinks. Pins go in after the coils, angled down, one every 4 in.

Wind coils on a 1/2 in rod in a drill at low speed, counting turns; cut to the measured resistance with a meter, not to length, since wire varies. Stretch each coil evenly to the groove length before laying it in; a bunched coil runs hot and fails there.
Wire the control circuit so that the high limit, the door switch and the emergency stop are all in series with the contactor coil: any one open and the elements are dead regardless of the controller.
First fire empty to 1,000 F over four hours with the door cracked an inch until 400 F to drive moisture out of the brick and mortar; let the controller autotune at 900 F with the shelf in.

Soda-lime annealing: hold at 900 to 960 F long enough for the thickest section (about an hour per half inch), then cool 50 to 100 F an hour to 700 F and 150 to 250 F an hour to 300 F; thick casting goes far slower. The controller's segments carry the schedule; the glass never meets a draft from an opened door above 400 F.

equipment.name: Glory hole, 16 in bore, forced-air gas
equipment.summary: A horizontal reheating chamber 16 in in diameter and 26 in deep: a 1 in cast 3,000 F hot face over 3 in of 2,600 F fiber blanket inside a 24 in diameter rolled steel shell, a cast back wall with a tangential burner port, a cast door ring with two half-moon doors on a foot-pedal pivot (pneumatic cylinders optional), on an adjustable stand. One forced-air burner of 150,000 to 250,000 BTU/h on natural gas at 7 inches of water column or propane at 11, a combustion air blower with a butterfly valve, a pilot, a flame safeguard and a gas train to the National Fuel Gas Code. It runs at 2,100 to 2,300 F and idles on about 100,000 BTU/h with the doors shut.

build_notes: Roll or cut the shell, weld the back disc with its burner port and the front ring; weld the anchors to the inside before any blanket goes in.

Lay the blanket in two layers with staggered seams, then set the 16 in sonotube form on centre with spacers and cast the hot face in one pour, rodding out the air; cast the back wall with the burner-block plug in place at the tangent angle, and the doors in their frames face down on melamine.

Cure 24 hours under plastic, strip the forms, and dry on the first fire: 50 F an hour to 250 F with a 4 hour hold, 50 F an hour to 500 F with a 4 hour hold, then 100 F an hour to 1,500 F. Fiber shrinks and castable steams; both want the slow first day.

Fire the burner outside the chamber first and set the orifice and air; then into the block. A tangential flame should wrap the bore and leave the opening as a lazy roll, not a jet; too much air and the bore goes dull and roars, too little and the doors soot.
Set the door stop so a blowpipe passes with 2 in to spare; set the foot pedal so a full press opens the doors fully and a half press reaches the stop.
The idle setting is the one that pays the gas bill: find the lowest fire that holds a dull orange bore with the doors shut and mark the needle valve.
